subject: 장기는 누구에게 먼저 가야 하는가
title: Deciding who receives the organ
content: When an organ becomes available and several patients could use it, somebody must choose, and every choice is a moral judgment rather than a technical one. The criteria that different systems apply reveal quite different views about justice, and examining them exposes disagreements that ordinarily stay buried. One criterion is medical urgency: the organ goes to whoever will die soonest without it. This has obvious moral appeal, since it treats saving a life as the governing value. Yet urgency correlates with poor condition, so the sickest patient may also be least likely to survive the operation, and a system following urgency alone may waste organs that would have saved somebody else. A second criterion is expected benefit, measured in years of life gained. This maximises the good obtained from a scarce resource, and yet it systematically disadvantages older patients and those with other conditions, which many regard as a failure of equal respect rather than an efficient allocation. A third criterion is waiting time, which treats every patient alike and cannot be manipulated. Its weakness is that it ignores everything relevant, including whether the transplant will work. Most systems combine these, and the weights they assign are moral decisions presented as clinical protocol. More contested still is whether conduct should count. Proposals to deprioritise patients whose illness followed their own choices appeal to desert, and they are resisted on the ground that medicine should not adjudicate blame, particularly since the conduct in question is distributed unevenly across circumstances nobody chose. What the whole debate demonstrates is that scarcity forces a society to state what it believes about equal worth. A committee dividing organs is answering a question about justice under a name that makes it sound like triage, and the honest response is to publish the criteria so that they can be argued about rather than merely applied.

subject: 의사의 양심과 환자의 요구
title: When a clinician refuses on principle
content: A patient requests a lawful procedure and the clinician declines because they hold it to be wrong. Such conflicts arise around the end of life, around reproduction, and elsewhere, and they set two genuine moral claims against each other rather than pitting a principle against mere preference. The clinician's claim rests on integrity. Requiring somebody to perform an act they regard as seriously wrong asks them to act against their own moral judgment, and a society that values conscience cannot dismiss this lightly. Professions have historically protected such refusals, and the protection is not merely a concession to religious groups but a recognition that moral agency does not stop at the surgery door. The patient's claim rests on access and on standing. They are entitled to a lawful service, they may live where alternatives are distant, and being refused by the person they approached carries a message about their choices that no leaflet removes. Where refusals are common in a region, a formal entitlement becomes unavailable in practice, and a right nobody can exercise is not much of a right. Most workable arrangements separate refusing to perform from obstructing. A clinician may decline the act while being required to say so early, to avoid moral commentary, and to ensure the patient reaches somebody who will assist. This preserves integrity without transferring its cost to the person seeking care. The arrangement fails in two directions. Where referral itself is regarded as complicity, no compromise remains, and the system must decide whose claim yields. Where refusals are numerous enough to close access entirely, the individual accommodation has produced a collective denial, and justice then requires attending to the pattern rather than to each case.

subject: 정물화의 상징 체계
title: Objects arranged to be read
content: A still life presents a table of ordinary things, and viewers unfamiliar with the tradition see only skill in rendering surfaces. Contemporaries of the great Dutch examples saw considerably more, since the objects were selected from a shared vocabulary and their arrangement made an argument. Learning that vocabulary transforms the pictures. A skull, a guttering candle, a watch, and cut flowers all indicate the brevity of life, and their presence turns a display of abundance into a warning about it. Soap bubbles carry the same meaning, and so does a book left open at a page nobody will finish. The genre containing these signs was named for the moral it delivered, and its popularity coincided with an era of sudden commercial wealth, which is not a coincidence. Other objects announce that wealth directly. Lemons imported at great cost, porcelain from the far side of the world, silver vessels, and glass of a fineness only certain workshops could produce all declare the reach of trade. A painting could therefore celebrate prosperity and warn against attachment to it simultaneously, and the tension between those messages is what gives the strongest examples their peculiar seriousness. The rendering itself carried meaning. Painters competed at depicting the specific difficulty of each surface: the fog on a grape, the dulling of pewter, the transparency of a half filled glass. Such passages were understood as demonstrations, and clients paid for the demonstration as much as for the subject. Reading these pictures now requires reconstructing what their first audience knew without effort. The tradition assumed that viewers would recognise a flower blooming in the wrong season, or a beetle placed on a leaf, and the meanings attached to such details have to be recovered from emblem books and inventories rather than from the paintings themselves.

subject: 생물 다양성의 값
title: Why the number of kinds should matter
content: Arguments for preserving the variety of living kinds usually appeal to what that variety supplies. Species yield medicines, stabilise the systems that produce food, and support activities people pay for, therefore losing them is costly. Such reasoning is true and effective, and yet many who advance it hold a further conviction that it does not express. The instrumental argument has a weakness that its defenders rarely acknowledge. If value derives from usefulness, then a kind supplying nothing has no claim, and the case for preserving it collapses. Worse, the argument invites the reply that a substitute would do, since what is wanted is the function rather than the particular thing performing it. Anybody who believes the loss would be regrettable regardless is committed to something the argument does not contain. One further claim points to knowledge. Each distinct kind embodies a solution to the problem of living somewhere, worked out over an enormous span, and losing it destroys information nobody has recorded. This is still instrumental, although it concerns a use we cannot yet specify, which weakens the demand that benefits be demonstrated in advance. A stronger claim holds that the value is not ours to assign. A kind that has persisted for millions of years has a standing that does not depend on being noticed, and the moral case for restraint rests on what such things are rather than on what they do for us. Defending this position is harder, since it appeals to a value that no transaction registers. The practical stakes are considerable. An argument built entirely on usefulness will lose whenever a more profitable use appears, and conservation defended on those grounds is permanently negotiable. Recognising a value that our purposes did not create changes what the argument is about, which may be the only ground that holds.

subject: 가면극의 인물 유형
title: Characters that everyone already knows
content: Masked theatre traditions across many cultures work with a fixed set of characters rather than inventing new ones for each play. The audience recognises the mask, knows immediately what the figure wants and how it will behave, and the drama proceeds from that shared knowledge rather than from exposition. Understanding why this arrangement is powerful requires setting aside the assumption that originality is the point. A fixed type carries its whole history into the performance. When the boastful soldier enters, the audience brings every previous appearance with them, so the performer may begin at a level of complexity that a new character could not reach in an evening. Departures then become expressive. A miser who briefly shows generosity produces an effect available only because the type made the departure visible. The masks themselves encode the information. Their features are exaggerated in ways that carry meaning at a distance, and a tradition's audiences learn the vocabulary early, so identification is instant. Because the face cannot change, the performer must convey feeling through the body, and traditions using masks develop a physical technique that unmasked acting rarely demands. This produces a distinctive aesthetic rather than a limitation. The Italian tradition of improvised comedy shows how far the method can be pushed. Performers held no script, only a plot outline and the type they had played for years, and the evening was constructed live from remembered routines fitted to the situation. Such work is impossible without types, since improvisation needs a shared frame. Related structures appear in Japanese, Korean, and West African performance, each with its own stock figures and its own conventions about what a mask may do. The recurrence across unconnected cultures suggests that the arrangement solves a genuine problem in how a performance communicates with an audience quickly.

subject: 번역된 시가 잃는 것
title: What survives when a poem changes language
content: A poem translated into another language becomes a different object. Prose survives the crossing reasonably well, since its meaning can be carried by a different arrangement of words, but poetry binds meaning to sound, rhythm, and the particular associations that words carry in one tradition and not another. The translator must therefore decide what to save. Sound is usually the first casualty. A pattern of rhyme in the original cannot ordinarily be reproduced without changing which words appear, so the translator either abandons the pattern or abandons the literal sense. Both choices are defensible and neither is free. Versions preserving the metre frequently read as strained, while versions preserving the meaning read as prose broken into lines. Association is the deeper loss. A word in one language carries a history of use, appearing in familiar texts and songs, and this accumulated weight is invisible in a dictionary. A translator can find an accurate equivalent that arrives with entirely different associations, so the line is correct and the effect is gone. Some traditions attach meanings to particular flowers, colours, or seasons that a reader elsewhere simply does not have. Several strategies have developed in response. Some translators produce a plain version accompanied by extensive notes, treating the poem as something to be studied. Others write a new poem in the target language that attempts a comparable effect, which produces work of literary value while departing considerably from the original. A few present the original alongside, admitting that the translation is a guide rather than a substitute. What the difficulty reveals is how much of a poem is made of its language rather than expressed in it. This is why the art travels less easily than music or painting, and why cultures separated by language know each other's poetry far less well than they know each other's other arts.

subject: 아이누의 수렵 채집 전통
title: A people who kept to the forest and the river
content: The Ainu of the northern islands maintained a way of life based on hunting, fishing, and gathering long after farming had spread across the region to the south. Their history has been recovered slowly, partly because outsiders wrote most of the early accounts and partly because the community itself was pressed hard by the state that absorbed its territory. Their subsistence rested on the salmon run, on deer, and on the bear, and the seasonal round moved between coast and inland valleys. Because they did not farm, earlier writers described them as primitive, applying a scale that ranks ways of life by how they obtain food. Archaeology has undermined that ranking, since the settlements show substantial dwellings, extensive exchange with neighbours to the south, and a material culture of considerable elaboration. Their ceremonial life centred on relations with animals. A bear taken as a cub was raised in the settlement and then sent back to the spirit world in an elaborate rite, and the ceremony expressed an understanding in which animals visit people as guests bearing meat and fur, receiving hospitality and gifts in return. Such a view organises hunting as an exchange rather than as extraction. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries brought severe disruption. The territory was annexed, hunting and fishing were restricted, the language was suppressed in schools, and assimilation was pursued as policy. The language now has very few first speakers, although recovery efforts have grown. Recognition as an indigenous people came only in recent decades. What the case illustrates is how a civilization's history gets written by whoever prevailed. For a long period the Ainu appeared in scholarship as a remnant to be explained rather than as a people with their own account, and the correction of that record is recent and incomplete.

subject: 활자체가 만드는 목소리
title: How letterforms speak before the words do
content: Every printed text arrives in a particular typeface, and readers absorb an impression from the letterforms before processing a single word. This effect is largely unconscious, which is exactly why it works, and typographic design is among the least noticed of the applied arts. The historical associations do much of the work. Forms derived from Roman inscriptions and Renaissance printing carry authority and tradition, while geometric letterforms designed in the twentieth century carry an association with modernity and rational design. A reader need know none of this history, since the associations were absorbed from where the forms are habitually used. A legal document set in the modern face and an advertisement set in the classical one both feel subtly wrong. Practical qualities matter as much. Small serifs at the ends of strokes assist the eye along a line, which is why long passages of print have traditionally used them, and generous space between letters improves reading on screens where resolution is limited. The choice of a face for a novel is therefore a decision about how the reading will feel over three hundred pages, and publishers have preferred certain designs for exactly that reason for a century. Type also carries cultural specificity. Scripts other than the Latin alphabet have their own traditions of proportion and stroke, and designing a face that works across several scripts requires reconciling systems that developed independently. The results are frequently compromises, and communities whose script is treated as an extension of a Latin design have reasonable complaints about it. What the field demonstrates is that a purely functional craft accumulates an aesthetic vocabulary. Nobody set out to make certain letterforms mean tradition and others mean progress, and yet a century of use established those meanings so firmly that a designer cannot now escape them.

subject: 알고리즘이 내리는 결정의 정당성
title: When a procedure decides about a person
content: Decisions about loans, hiring, and release from custody are increasingly made or shaped by statistical procedures. Defenders point out that such procedures are consistent, cheap, and free of the moods and prejudices that affect human judgment. These advantages are genuine, and yet several moral objections survive them. The first concerns what the procedure does. A statistical model predicts an outcome from features associated with it in past data, which means it treats the individual as a member of a reference class. Somebody refused because people resembling them defaulted has not been assessed as themselves, and the objection that they are not a statistic is a moral claim rather than a technical complaint. The second concerns inherited injustice. Where past decisions were unfair, the record of those decisions is the training material, and a procedure fitted to it reproduces the pattern while presenting the result as neutral computation. Removing the obvious variable does not help, since other features correlate with it. Consequently the appearance of objectivity is exactly what makes the mechanism dangerous. The third concerns explanation. A person adversely affected has a claim to know why, and some procedures cannot supply reasons in any form a person could contest. Losing the ability to argue with a decision removes something that justice supplies even where the decision was correct. Against all this stands the alternative. Human decisions in the same domains have been demonstrably inconsistent and biased, so rejecting the procedure returns the matter to a process with its own serious defects. The honest position is therefore comparative rather than absolute. What can be demanded is that such systems be tested for disparate outcomes, that reasons be produced, and that a person may appeal to a human being who has the authority to disagree with the model.

subject: 반복 구조로 짓는 배경 음악
title: Music written to be heard many times
content: Music composed for spaces where people spend hours faces a problem that concert music does not. It must remain tolerable across long exposure, support attention directed elsewhere, and avoid producing fatigue in listeners who did not choose to hear it. The traditions that developed for games and for public spaces solve this problem with distinctive techniques. Repetition is the central difficulty. A piece looping for hours will become intolerable unless its repetition is handled carefully, so composers avoid strong melodic hooks that demand attention and design phrases whose ending flows into the beginning without a seam. Where the loop point is audible, listeners begin counting the cycles, and the music moves from background to irritant. A second technique layers the material. Rather than a single fixed piece, the music is assembled from parts that enter and leave according to what is happening, so the texture changes without any transition being composed. Listeners perceive variety while hearing a small amount of written material, and the underlying harmony can remain constant for long periods without seeming static. Modal harmony assists, since progressions that avoid strong resolution can continue indefinitely. The aesthetic result is distinctive rather than merely functional. Composers working under these constraints developed a style prizing texture over melody and gradual change over event, and the best work in the tradition rewards close listening despite having been designed for inattention. Several such scores have been performed in concert, which produces the odd situation of an audience attending to music built to be ignored. What the field illustrates is how a practical requirement can produce an artistic language. Nothing about a game demanded modal harmony and seamless looping, and yet the requirement to be heard fifty times without wearing out led composers toward a specific and now recognisable sound.

subject: 공공 조각과 장소의 관계
title: A sculpture that belongs to its site
content: A work placed in a public square differs from one in a gallery in ways that go beyond scale. Nobody chose to encounter it, everybody passes it repeatedly, and it will outlast the debates that produced it. These conditions make public sculpture a distinctive art with its own criteria of success. The relation to the site is the central question. A work conceived independently and then placed somewhere convenient sits in the square without belonging to it, whereas a work made for a particular position responds to sightlines, to the buildings around it, and to how people move through the space. Artists working in this tradition frequently describe the site as material rather than as a location, and removing such a work destroys it in a sense that moving a painting does not. Permanence creates its own difficulty. A commemorative monument fixes a judgment in bronze while the community's view of the subject continues to change, and the resulting conflicts have occupied many cities in recent years. Some responses remove the work, some add material that reframes it, and some leave it while changing what surrounds it. Each option makes a claim about whether public art should record what a society believed or what it now believes. Everyday use complicates matters further. People sit on sculpture, children climb it, and it acquires the marks of weather and of hands. Artists differ enormously in whether they regard this as damage or as completion, and a work designed to resist contact tends to read as unwelcoming. What distinguishes success in this art is therefore not the same as in a gallery. A public work must survive familiarity, since its audience will see it thousands of times, and pieces that reveal something new on the hundredth passing are rarer and more valuable than those that impress once.

subject: 축제의 주기와 공동체
title: Why a community marks the same days each year
content: Festivals return on a schedule, and their recurrence is not incidental to what they accomplish. A celebration held once would be an event; one held every year at the same point becomes an instrument by which a community measures time and recognises itself. The cultural work is done by the repetition rather than by any single occasion. Most such cycles attach to the agricultural year or to the sky. Harvest, sowing, the longest night, and the return of light appear across unconnected traditions, because these were the moments when a settled people faced either relief or anxiety together. Even where the original occasion has become irrelevant to how people live, the date frequently survives, absorbed into a later tradition that kept the timing while changing the meaning. The activities are strikingly consistent across cultures. Special food, suspended ordinary rules, costume, and licensed reversal of everyday roles appear repeatedly, and the reversal is particularly interesting. Festivals in which servants are served, or authority is mocked, occur widely, and they seem to release pressure that ordinary hierarchy accumulates without threatening the hierarchy itself. Participation matters more than performance. A festival is something a community does rather than watches, and traditions that shift toward spectacle, with most people observing while a few perform, frequently report that the occasion has lost its force. This is a common complaint where tourism has become the main audience. What the cycle finally provides is a shared calendar of memory. Somebody returning after decades finds the same day marked in the same way, and the continuity connects them to people long dead who did the same things at the same point in the year. Few cultural forms accomplish that as economically, which may explain why festivals survive changes of religion, of government, and of livelihood.

subject: 자작나무 껍질 문서의 도시
title: Letters written on bark in a medieval city
content: In the wet clay under the medieval city of Novgorod lie documents written on birch bark. More than a thousand have been recovered since the first was found in the middle of the twentieth century, and they have transformed what can be said about ordinary life in that era of eastern Europe. Bark was cheap. Parchment was costly and reserved for important texts, so people used the inner layer of birch for anything transient, scratching letters with a metal stylus. The material rots in dry ground but survives indefinitely in waterlogged clay, therefore this ancient city preserves a class of document that has vanished almost everywhere else. What the letters contain is remarkable precisely because it is trivial. A merchant asks about a debt, a woman arranges a marriage, a son demands money from his father, a labourer complains that he has not been paid, and a boy named Onfim covers a sheet with drawings of horsemen mixed with his alphabet practice. Almost none of this material would have been thought worth writing on parchment. The evidence has settled a long argument. Historians had assumed that literacy in the region was confined to clergy and to a narrow elite, and the letters demonstrate otherwise, since they were written and read by merchants, craftsmen, women, and children across several centuries. Handwriting varies from practised to laborious, which is itself evidence about how widely the skill had spread. The city that produced them was unusual in its politics as well, governed by an assembly that hired and dismissed its princes. When it was absorbed by a rising power to the south in the fifteenth century, that arrangement ended. The bark documents remain the fullest surviving record of how ordinary people in a medieval city actually conducted their affairs.

subject: 추천 체계와 자율성
title: Being shown what you will probably choose
content: Systems that select what a person sees next now shape a large portion of reading, listening, and viewing. Their designers describe them as serving preferences, and in an obvious sense they do, since they are built to predict what will hold attention. The moral question is whether serving preferences in this way respects the person or undermines something about them. Autonomy involves more than getting what one currently wants. It involves forming and revising one's wants, and doing so requires encountering things one would not have selected. A system optimising for immediate engagement narrows the range of encounters by construction, therefore it may satisfy present preferences while restricting the process by which preferences change. Nothing about this requires any intention to manipulate. A second consideration concerns whose interest the prediction serves. The system is not built to make the person's life go well; it is built to maximise a measure that its operator chose, and attention captured is not the same as value delivered. Where those diverge, the person is being served in a sense that the word conceals. Defenders reply that people remain free to look elsewhere, and that treating adults as unable to resist a suggestion is condescending. This has force, although it underestimates how much the default matters, since evidence across many domains shows that what is presented first is chosen overwhelmingly often. A moral response need not demand abolition. Making the ranking criterion visible, letting a person adjust it, and building in deliberate variety are all available, and their absence is a design decision rather than a technical necessity. What the case shows is that a system can respect stated preferences while damaging the capacity that gives preferences their value, and that the language of choice can conceal exactly this.

subject: 차 문화와 절제의 미
title: An aesthetic built on doing less
content: The tea ceremony as it developed in Japan takes an ordinary act and surrounds it with an elaborate discipline. Every movement is prescribed, the room is small and deliberately plain, and the whole occasion may last hours to produce a bowl of tea. Understanding why a culture invested such attention in this requires taking its aesthetic seriously rather than treating it as etiquette. The governing value prizes restraint over display. Objects used are frequently rough, asymmetrical, and marked by use, and a bowl with a visible repair may be valued above a flawless one. This preference developed partly in reaction to an earlier fashion for imported Chinese wares of great refinement, so the aesthetic carries an argument about what deserves admiration. Its central terms concern simplicity, weathering, and the beauty available in what is incomplete. The architecture enforces the attitude. The room is small enough to bring participants close, the entrance is low so that everybody must bow to pass through, and the decoration consists of a single scroll and a single arrangement of flowers changed for each occasion. Nothing competes for attention, which makes small things perceptible: the sound of water, the change of light, the particular character of one utensil. Time is handled deliberately. The pace is slower than any practical purpose requires, and the guest who arrives impatient will find the occasion tedious. What the discipline cultivates is a quality of attention that ordinary life does not permit, and the tradition holds that this attention is the point rather than the tea. Related aesthetics appear in gardens, in poetry, and in ceramics from the same culture, and the connections are explicit rather than coincidental. The tradition is a coherent argument that beauty is found by removing rather than by adding, worked out across several arts over centuries.

subject: 직물 문양의 전승
title: Patterns carried in cloth across generations
content: Woven and embroidered patterns persist with remarkable stability across generations, and in many cultures a pattern identifies where its maker came from as precisely as a dialect does. Understanding how such traditions transmit reveals something about how any craft knowledge survives without written instruction. The transmission is physical rather than verbal. A girl learning to weave in a household where weaving happens watches, then assists, then works, and the pattern is stored in the sequence of actions rather than in any description. Consequently the knowledge is difficult to record and difficult to lose, since it is held in many hands at once. Where the practice stops for a generation, however, recovery is extremely hard, because nobody wrote down what everybody knew. Technique constrains design. A loom of a particular construction makes certain patterns easy and others impossible, so the visual tradition of a region reflects its equipment as much as its taste. Geometric designs dominate where the structure of the weave produces them naturally, while curved forms appear where embroidery is added after weaving. Reading a textile therefore involves reading the machine that made it. Patterns also carry information. In several traditions the arrangement marks a woman's home village, her marital status, or the occasion for which a garment was made, so the cloth functions as a document that its community reads without effort. Outsiders admiring the design frequently miss the statement entirely. What threatens such traditions is rarely a change of taste. Industrial production supplying cheaper cloth removes the practical reason to weave, and once the household no longer produces its own textiles the chain of transmission breaks within a generation. Revival efforts are common and difficult, since a pattern can be copied from a museum piece while the knowledge that generated it cannot.

subject: 광고는 어디까지 허용되는가
title: Where persuasion becomes something else
content: Advertising both informs and persuades, and each is normally permitted. Telling somebody that a product exists is useful, and urging them to prefer it is what anybody does who believes their goods are good. Yet many people hold that some advertising is morally wrong, and stating that objection precisely is harder than feeling it. One line falls between persuasion and manipulation. Persuasion works through a person’s reason, offering grounds they can weigh and reject. Manipulation works around that reason, using fear, habit, and a moment of inattention to plant a want the person would not own if they stopped to think. The line is genuine, although drawing it is hard, since much ordinary speech mixes both and an appeal to feeling is not wrong by itself. A second line falls at truth. Plain lying is barred nearly everywhere, and yet a great deal of advertising builds a false picture through what it selects, what it implies, and what it shows, while every stated claim stays accurate. If the moral fault in lying lies in planting a false belief on purpose, then such work is dishonest whatever the small print says. A third line falls at the audience. Persuading a grown adult differs from targeting a child, who cannot yet see that they are being sold to, or people whose circumstances make one offer hard to refuse. Many places restrict advertising to children for that very reason, and the same ground plainly reaches further than it is now applied. A fourth concern is the sheer mass of it. One notice may be harmless while a world saturated with them shapes what a whole culture values, and that harm has no author. So no blanket verdict is available. The defensible objections are narrow ones, and stating them exactly makes a stronger moral case than any broad complaint about commerce ever does.

subject: 민화의 유형과 변형
title: Pictures painted by name-less hands
content: Alongside the painting produced for courts and temples, most cultures developed a popular tradition made by unnamed artisans for ordinary households. Such work has frequently been dismissed as crude imitation of higher art, and closer study shows something more interesting: a body of images with its own conventions, its own purposes, and its own logic of variation. The subjects repeat because they are functional. Certain animals bring protection, certain plants bring long life or many children, and a painting hung in a particular room performs a particular job. Consequently the painter is not seeking novelty, and a client asking for the customary subject expects the customary treatment. What varies is handling, and within a fixed subject the range of solutions across surviving examples is enormous. The relation to elite painting is not simple copying. Motifs certainly travelled downward, and yet popular versions frequently transform what they borrow, flattening space, brightening colour, and abandoning the restraint that the trained tradition valued. Tigers rendered by court painters look dangerous; the same animal in the popular tradition frequently looks comic, and the transformation appears deliberate rather than incompetent. Anonymity shaped the whole practice. Painters did not sign, workshops repeated designs, and value attached to whether the picture did its job rather than to who made it. This is why such work entered museums late, since the collecting tradition was organised around named artists and had no category for excellent painting by nobody in particular. Modern reassessment has been substantial. The visual qualities that once counted as failings — flat space, bold colour, cheerful distortion — are now recognised as a coherent aesthetic, and several twentieth century artists studied this tradition deliberately. The reassessment says as much about changing taste as about the paintings themselves.

subject: 판소리에서 청중이 하는 일
title: An audience that answers back
content: In the Korean tradition of sung storytelling, a single performer delivers a story lasting several hours, accompanied by one drummer. What distinguishes the form from other narrative arts is that the audience is expected to participate, calling out encouragement at appropriate moments, and a performance without such calls is regarded as having failed. The calls are conventional rather than spontaneous shouting. Certain phrases are used, they arrive at particular points in the musical phrase, and skilled listeners place them where they support the singer rather than interrupt. The drummer supplies them as well, so the accompaniment is partly verbal. Consequently the performance is a collaboration in which the boundary between stage and audience is deliberately incomplete. This has consequences for how the art works. A singer receiving strong response will extend a passage, and one meeting silence may move on, so the length and shape of a performance vary with the room. The written texts that survive are therefore records of one realisation rather than fixed scores, and comparing versions transmitted through different lineages shows substantial variation in the same story. The vocal technique is demanding in a specific way. The tradition prizes a rough, strained quality achieved through years of training, and the sound is deliberately far from the smooth production that other singing traditions cultivate. A voice that is too beautiful is regarded as unsuited to the material, since the stories concern hardship and the sound is expected to carry it. What the form illustrates is a different understanding of what a performance is. Rather than a finished object presented to observers, it is an occasion produced by everyone present, and the culture surrounding it treats knowing how and when to call out as a skill worth acquiring rather than as mere enthusiasm.

subject: 명대 항해와 대형 선박
title: The fleets that sailed and then stopped
content: In the early fifteenth century the Ming court sent out a series of enormous fleets that reached south east Asia, India, Arabia, and the east coast of Africa. The expeditions carried tens of thousands of men in hundreds of vessels, and the largest ships described in the records would have been among the biggest wooden vessels ever built. Then the voyages ended, the records were neglected, and the capacity was allowed to lapse. The purpose was not conquest or ordinary commerce. The fleets carried gifts, collected tribute, escorted rulers to the capital, and returned with exotic animals, and their function was to display the reach of the empire and to enrol distant courts in a relationship of formal deference. Consequently they were expensive without producing the kind of return that trade produces, and the expense became an argument against them. The ending has attracted more attention than the voyages. Officials at court had opposed the programme from the beginning, partly on cost and partly because the eunuch establishment that ran it competed with them for influence. A shift of attention toward the northern frontier, where a land threat was real and pressing, made the maritime programme look like an indulgence. Ships were left to rot and the shipyards declined. What makes the episode significant in world history is the comparison it invites. Within decades European vessels far smaller than these were rounding Africa, and the difference in outcome is frequently attributed to technology when the record suggests it was a matter of what each state decided to pursue. The capacity existed and was set aside. Historians disagree about how far the ending should be read as a failure of vision or as a rational choice given the empire's actual threats, and the disagreement turns on values as much as on evidence.

subject: 블루스 음계의 이동
title: The notes that slide between the keys
content: Blues singing and playing use pitches that lie between the notes available on a keyboard. A performer bends toward a note without arriving, or approaches it from below and settles slightly under it, and these inflections are not approximations of the written pitch but the substance of the style. Notation cannot record them, which has caused persistent confusion. Early attempts to write the music down produced a scale with certain degrees marked as flattened, and the description has been taught ever since. It is misleading, since the pitch is not a fixed lowered note but a region through which the voice or the string moves. Recordings show performers placing the same degree differently within a single phrase, and the variation carries expressive weight rather than indicating imprecision. The instruments reflect this. Guitar technique in the tradition developed bending and sliding as fundamental resources, and the bottleneck slide exists precisely to reach pitches between the frets. Harmonica players developed a technique for lowering notes below their fixed pitch. Where a piano is used, players approximate the effect by striking adjacent keys together, which produces a comparable ambiguity through different means. The origins of these practices have been argued about for a long time, with proposals connecting them to West African vocal traditions where similar inflection appears. What is clear is that the resulting music does not fit the European framework it is usually described within, and that describing it in those terms has flattened it in scholarship and in teaching. The influence on later music has been enormous. Most popular styles of the past century inherited these inflections, and performers who never encountered the original tradition use them constantly, which makes this among the most widely transmitted aesthetic innovations of modern times.

subject: 최저임금을 정당화하는 논거
title: Arguments for a floor under wages
content: A legal minimum wage prevents certain agreements between willing parties, and defending it therefore requires explaining why those particular agreements should be forbidden. The arguments offered fall into several types, and they rest on quite different moral foundations. The first appeals to bargaining position. A worker with no savings and no alternative accepts whatever is offered, and calling the result a free agreement misdescribes it, since one party could walk away and the other could not. On this view the floor corrects a defect in the conditions of consent rather than overriding a genuine choice. The second appeals to what work should provide. If somebody works full time, the argument holds, they should not need public assistance to survive, and an employer paying less is having their wage bill subsidised by everybody else. This reframes the question, since the alternative to a floor is not lower cost but a cost paid elsewhere. The third appeals to dignity. A wage below a certain level communicates something about how the worker is regarded, and a society permitting it accepts a hierarchy in which some people's labour is treated as nearly worthless. This is a claim about standing rather than about income. The objection is economic and serious. If a floor is set above what an employer will pay, some jobs disappear, and those losing them are the least skilled workers the measure was meant to help. Evidence on the size of this effect is genuinely mixed and depends heavily on the level chosen. What follows is that the moral case is strong while the practical question of where to set the floor cannot be answered from principle alone. Treating the empirical dispute as though it settled the moral one, or the reverse, has made this argument considerably less productive than it should be.

subject: 무용 기보법의 시도와 실패
title: The notations that dance never adopted
content: Several complete systems for writing down dance exist, some of them worked out with great care over decades, and a trained reader can reconstruct a work from their pages. Almost no company uses them. Examining the specific systems, rather than the general problem, shows why an art form might decline an apparently useful tool. The earliest surviving attempts recorded floor patterns, drawing the path a dancer traced through the room with symbols along the line indicating steps. This suited court dances where the figure made by the group was the point. It became useless as the art moved toward what individual bodies do rather than where they go. Two twentieth century systems took different approaches to that problem. One uses a vertical staff read from the bottom, with columns for each part of the body and symbol shapes indicating direction while their length indicates duration. The other places abstract signs on a stave representing the body seen from behind, adding indications of the path and of relationships between dancers. Both are complete, both have been used to record major works, and both require months of study to read fluently. The barrier is that investment. A choreographer can teach a company a piece in the time it would take a notator to record it, and the company can retain it through rehearsal. The notation solves a problem that arises only decades later, when everybody who danced it is gone, and institutions rarely fund work whose benefit arrives after the funders have retired. Video appeared to solve the problem cheaply and did not, since a recording preserves one cast's performance and cannot show what was essential rather than incidental. Companies that maintain a historical repertoire have learned this, and the small number of trained notators now working are employed almost entirely by them.

subject: 캐리커처와 풍자의 한계
title: Drawing somebody worse than they are
content: Caricature exaggerates a person's features to make an argument about their character. The technique is ancient, the modern tradition of political drawing dates from the era of cheap printing, and the form has always operated close to a boundary that its practitioners argue about among themselves. The technique works through recognition. A caricaturist identifies whatever makes a face distinctive and enlarges it, and viewers identify the subject faster from the drawing than from a photograph, because the exaggeration isolates what the eye uses. This is why the art can be devastating: it claims to reveal what the person actually is by amplifying what they visibly are. The moral difficulty lies in that claim. Exaggerating a politician's jaw to suggest stubbornness makes an argument about their conduct through their appearance, and the connection between the two is asserted rather than demonstrated. Where the feature exaggerated is one the subject shares with a group, the drawing borrows whatever contempt attaches to that group, and the history of the form contains a great deal of this. Some of the most technically brilliant work in the tradition is also its most poisonous. Practitioners generally locate the boundary at power. Caricature directed upward, at those who hold authority and can answer back, performs a function that few other arts perform, and its cruelty is licensed by the target's position. The same technique directed at people with no platform is simply an attack, and the aesthetic accomplishment does not redeem it. What the case illustrates is that a technique can be morally neutral while its application is not. The skill of finding what is characteristic in a face is the same skill in both directions, which is precisely why the tradition has spent two centuries arguing about where to point it.
